children.text: tathā hi dūrādrūpaṃ paśyatīti ||
children.translated_text: For indeed one sees a form from afar.

children.text: yatra rūpaṃ dṛśyate na tatra tadgrāhakaṃ cakṣurindriyam asti tatra pramāṇānupalabhyamānatvāt tatrāvidyamānadevadattādivat ||
children.translated_text: Where a form is seen, the visual sense faculty that apprehends it is not present, because no means of knowledge establishes its presence there, just as in the case of <s>Devadatta</s> and others who are absent from that place.

children.text: yathā cakṣuḥ evaṃ śrotramapi vaktavyam ||
children.translated_text: What has been said of the eye should also be said of the ear.

children.text: itara āha svaviṣayadeśaprāpi cakṣuḥśrotram indriyatvāt ghrāṇendriyādivat ||
children.translated_text: The opponent says: “The eye and ear reach the location of their respective objects, because they are sense faculties, like the olfactory faculty and the others.”

children.text: anenānumānena tatra pramāṇānupalabhyamānatvaṃ hetum asiddhaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By this inference he shows that the reason, “because no means of knowledge establishes its presence there,” is unproven.

children.text: ācārya āha sati ca prāptaviṣayatva iti ||
children.translated_text: The Teacher says, “And if they operated on objects with which they make contact...”

children.text: vistaraḥ yadi prāptaviṣayaṃ cakṣuḥśrotraṃ kalpyeta divyaṃ cakṣuḥśrotramiha manuṣyeṣu dhyāyināṃ nopajāyeta ||
children.translated_text: The expanded statement is this: If the eye and ear were supposed to operate on objects with which they make contact, divine sight and hearing would not arise here among human meditators.

children.text: yadi hi cakṣuḥśrotram ativiprakṛṣṭadeśasthaṃ vyavahitaṃ ca kuḍyādibhiryathāyogaṃ rūpaṃ śabdaṃ gṛhṇīyād evamasya divyatvaṃ sambhavet tacca prāptaviṣayatve na syāt ||
children.translated_text: For if the eye and ear could respectively apprehend a form and a sound situated exceedingly far away and obstructed by a wall or the like, their divine character could thereby be possible; but this would not be possible if they operated only on objects with which they make contact.

children.text: prāṇādivat ||
children.translated_text: It is as with the olfactory faculty and the others.

children.text: yathā ghrāṇajihvākāyāḥ prāptaviṣayatvād divyā dhyāyināṃ nopajāyeran tadvat ||
children.translated_text: Just as divine faculties of smell, taste, and touch would not arise in meditators because those faculties operate on objects with which they make contact, so it is here.

children.text: anena svaviṣayadeśaprāpitvapakṣasya dharmiviśeṣaviparyayāpakṣālatvaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By this he shows that the thesis that the faculties reach the locations of their respective objects is vulnerable to the reversal of a distinctive property of the subject.

children.text: sambhavaddivyatve hi cakṣuḥśrotre dharmī ||
children.translated_text: For the subject consists of the eye and ear, in which divine capacity is possible.

children.text: asaṃbhavaddivyatvabhāvo viśeṣaviparyayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The reversal of the distinctive property is the condition in which divine capacity is impossible.

children.text: sa prāpnotīti doṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The fault is that this consequence follows.

children.text: anena doṣeṇānanumānatvāt tatpramāṇānupalabhyamānatvaṃ siddhaṃ vyavasthāpayati ||
children.translated_text: Since the argument is not an inference because of this fault, he establishes that the reason, “because no means of knowledge establishes their presence there,” is proven.

children.text: tasmādaprāptaviṣayaṃ cakṣuḥśrotram ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the eye and ear operate on objects without making contact with them.

children.text: yadyaprāptaviṣayaṃ cakṣuriti vistaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The expanded objection beginning, “If the eye operates on an object without making contact with it...” follows.

children.text: āsannenātidūrasthena tiraskṛtena vā tulyā tadaprāptiriti tatra darśanaṃ prasañjayati ||
children.translated_text: Since its lack of contact is the same with a nearby object, an exceedingly distant object, or an obstructed object, the objection entails that perception should occur in all three cases.

children.text: kimidaṃ parasya sādhanam uta dūṣaṇamiti yadi tāvadevaṃ sādhanam atidūraṃ tiraskṛtaṃ cakṣuḥśrotreṇa gṛhyate aprāptatvāt āsannaviṣayavat iti tadasādhanam hetoḥ svayamaniścitatvāt pūrvābhyupagamavirodhād vā ||
children.translated_text: Is this a proof offered by the opponent, or an objection? If it is first taken as a proof—“An exceedingly distant or obstructed object is apprehended by the eye and ear because they do not make contact with it, just as they apprehend a nearby object”—then it is no proof, because the reason is itself uncertain or because it contradicts what was previously admitted.

children.text: atha dūṣaṇam sarvāprāptagrāhakatvaṃ cakṣuḥśrotralakṣaṇasya dharmiṇaḥ prasajyate tad adūṣaṇam anumānabādhanāt ||
children.translated_text: If, on the other hand, it is an objection—“It follows that the subject characterized as the eye and ear apprehends every object with which it has no contact”—then it is no objection, because it is refuted by inference.

children.text: katham ityāha kathaṃ tāvad ayaskānto na sarvam aprāptam ayaḥ karṣatīti ||
children.translated_text: To explain how, he says: “How, then, does a magnet not draw every piece of iron with which it is not in contact?”

children.text: praśnamukhenāyaskāntanidarśanamupanyasya sarvāprāptagrāhakatvaṃ cakṣuḥśrotrasya sādhayati na sarvāprāptagrāhakaṃ cakṣuḥśrotram sarvāprāptagrahaṇaśaktihīnatvāt ayaskāntavat ||
children.translated_text: Having introduced the example of a magnet in the form of a question, he proves that the eye and ear do not apprehend every object with which they have no contact: “The eye and ear do not apprehend every non-contact object, because they lack the capacity to apprehend every such object, like a magnet.”

children.text: ayaskānto hyaprāptam ayo gṛhṇāti karṣatītyarthaḥ na ca sarvamaprāptaṃ gṛhṇāti tadvaccakṣuḥśrotram ||
children.translated_text: A magnet apprehends—that is, draws—iron with which it is not in contact, yet it does not apprehend every non-contact object; the eye and ear are likewise.

children.text: prāptaviṣayatve'pi caitat samānamiti ||
children.translated_text: This same consideration also applies if the faculties operate on objects with which they make contact.

children.text: nātidūratiraskṛto viṣayaścakṣuḥśrotreṇa gṛhyate grahaṇāyogyatvāt samprāptāñjanaśalākāvat ||
children.translated_text: An exceedingly distant or obstructed object is not apprehended by the eye and ear because it is unfit to be apprehended, just as a collyrium applicator brought into contact with the eye is not seen.

children.text: athavā na sarvasvagrāhyagrāhi cakṣuḥśrotram indriyasvābhāvyāt ghrāṇendriyādivat ||
children.translated_text: Alternatively: “The eye and ear do not apprehend every object proper to them, because this is the nature of sense faculties, like the olfactory faculty and the others.”

children.text: ghrāṇādīnāṃ hi prāpto viṣayo na tu sarvaḥ sahabhūgandhādyagrahaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: For the olfactory faculty and the others have objects with which they make contact, but they do not apprehend every such object, since they fail to apprehend odors and the other objects that coexist with them.

children.text: ghrāṇādisahabhūni hi gandharasaspraṣṭavyāni ghrāṇādibhirna gṛhyante śaktir hīndriyāṇām īdṛśīti ||
children.translated_text: Odors, tastes, and tangible objects that coexist with the olfactory faculty and the other faculties are not apprehended by those respective faculties, for such is the limited capacity of the faculties.

children.text: manastvarūpitvād iti ||
children.translated_text: But as for the mind, the text says, “because it is non-material.”

children.text: prāptatvaṃ mūrtānāmeva vyavasthāpyeta nāmūrtānāmiti ||
children.translated_text: Contact can be established only for material entities, not for immaterial ones.

children.text: mano'prāptaviṣayamiti na vicāraḥ kriyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, no inquiry is made into whether the mind operates on objects without making contact with them.
